items.line_paraphrase: Once the rest-day had ended, the three named women purchased aromatic spices intending to go and dress the body.
items.agent: Mary Magdalene, Mary mother of James, and Salome
items.outcome: spices in hand, with the intent to come and anoint him
items.narrator: anonymous third-person teller relating the women's actions

items.line_paraphrase: At daybreak on the week's first day they arrived at the burial place.
items.outcome: their arrival at the tomb at sunrise
items.narrator: same third-person teller, marking time and place

items.line_paraphrase: As they walked they were voicing a worry to one another.
items.outcome: the question uttered aloud among them
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's own speech

items.line_paraphrase: They ask who will move the sealing-stone aside for them.
items.substrate: the stone at the tomb's door
items.outcome: not-stated (open question, no answerer named)
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting their internal deliberation

items.line_paraphrase: Aside from the narrator: the stone was of great size.
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller in editorial aside, warranting the women's worry

items.line_paraphrase: Raising their eyes, they perceived that the stone had already been shifted aside.

items.outcome: their perception that the stone is already moved
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting what the women visually apprehend

items.line_paraphrase: The stone had already been moved back from the opening.
items.outcome: the opening now unblocked
items.narrator: third-person teller, reporting the perceived state (agent of the rolling unspecified)

items.line_paraphrase: Once inside the tomb, they saw a young figure seated to the right in a white robe.
items.operation: see (a young man sitting on the right, dressed in white)
items.substrate: M6a (the young man and his posture/attire)
items.outcome: their perception of an unexpected occupant
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's discovery inside the tomb

items.line_paraphrase: A young figure was seated on the right side, wearing a white robe.
items.operation: sit (dressed in white, on the right)
items.agent: not-stated (the young man is a topic, not a doer here)
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller inside the women's perception

items.line_paraphrase: They were struck with astonishment.
items.agent: not-stated (they undergo it, not perform it)
items.outcome: amazement as their state
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's reaction

items.line_paraphrase: The young figure addressed them.
items.outcome: his utterance directed at the women
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the young man's speech

items.line_paraphrase: He orders them to stop being astonished.
items.outcome: an imperative to release the fear
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man

items.line_paraphrase: He names whom they are looking for: the crucified Jesus of Nazareth.

items.outcome: the raising declared as accomplished; doer of the raising unnamed

items.line_paraphrase: He denies that he is present in the tomb.
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man's negation

items.line_paraphrase: He directs their attention to the spot where the body had been laid.
items.operation: direct-attention (behold the place where they laid him)
items.outcome: the women's gaze turned to the vacated place as evidence
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man

items.line_paraphrase: The messenger orders the women to depart.
items.substrate: the women (as those to be dispatched)
items.outcome: an imperative to leave the tomb on an errand
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man

items.line_paraphrase: He orders them to carry word to his followers, singling out Peter.

items.outcome: the women charged to relay the message to the disciples and Peter
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man

items.application_note: The move depends on the Jewish Sabbath-rest calendar making commerce impossible until the rest-day ends, hence the delayed purchase.
The timing 'first day of the week at dawn' presupposes the Jewish seven-day cultic week as the reckoning frame.
The anointing-errand and the sealed cave-tomb both presuppose Second-Temple Jewish burial practice with rolling-stone closure.
The need for outside help to move the closure-stone depends on the physical form of Judean rock-cut tombs of the period.
The narrator's aside about the stone's size only lands for hearers who know the tomb-closure convention it references.
The shock of the seen state depends on the hearer knowing a sealed tomb-stone was not supposed to be shiftable by the women.
Entering the burial chamber presupposes the rock-cut multi-chamber tomb-form of Second-Temple Judean practice.
The 'young man in white on the right' reads as an angelophany only within Jewish apocalyptic conventions of heavenly messengers.
The stunned-alarm response is the conventional human reaction to angelic epiphany in Jewish apocalyptic form.
The 'do not fear' formula is a fixed opening of angelic speech in Jewish apocalyptic literature.
Crucifixion as the mode of execution presupposes the Roman penal apparatus operating in Judea under Pax Romana.
'Raised from the dead' is intelligible only within Second-Temple Jewish resurrection-hope categories (Pharisaic/apocalyptic).
The denial 'he is not here' presupposes the burial-chamber norm where a corpse should be present for anointing.
Pointing to 'the place where they laid him' presupposes the specific ledge-form of a rock-cut Jewish burial niche.
'Going ahead to Galilee' depends on the concrete Jerusalem-to-Galilee geography and the community's northern homeland.
The promised seeing is anchored to the specific place 'there' — Galilee as a real geographic destination.
The 'trembling and astonishment' response follows Jewish apocalyptic conventions for reactions to epiphany.
Fear-silence terminating a gospel is a marked apocalyptic-literary convention, not a naturalistic report.
This verse opens the disputed longer ending — its very presence depends on the manuscript-transmission stratum of Markan tradition.
The 'first day of the week' dating presupposes the Jewish seven-day cultic week.
The Magdalene-first appearance harmonises with other resurrection traditions and is a hallmark of the added longer-ending stratum.
The claim 'he lives' is intelligible only within Second-Temple Jewish resurrection categories that make bodily post-mortem life sayable.
First-person seeing as warrant for a resurrection-claim depends on Jewish appearance-witness conventions taken over into early Christian kerygma.
The disciples' disbelief motif functions polemically to answer objections that resurrection-witness was uncritically accepted.
The Emmaus-style road-encounter is drawn from later synoptic tradition and marks this as a compilation-stratum ending.
The repeated disbelief motif serves the polemical function of pre-empting charges that the community were credulous.
The rebuke for hardness-of-heart functions internally against a rival stance that dismissed resurrection-witness testimony.
Grounding the rebuke in refusal-of-witnesses defends the chain of resurrection-testimony against outsider or insider skepticism.
'Go into all the world' presupposes Pax Romana travel-infrastructure that made Mediterranean-wide mission thinkable.
The universal-mission mandate rides on pre-existing Jewish diaspora networks as the seed-bed for early Christian expansion.
'Preach to every creature' presupposes the Gentile-mission horizon opened by Pauline-era contact with non-Jewish populations.
Baptism as the entry-rite of salvation presupposes the emerging Christian ritual system distinct from Temple cult.
'Signs accompanying believers' fits the Hellenistic-Jewish thoughtworld in which wonder-marks authenticate a divine messenger.
Exorcism 'in the name of' presupposes the Greco-Roman-Jewish name-invocation model of authority over unclean spirits.
Glossolalia as a missionary sign presupposes the multilingual Mediterranean contact-zone where 'new tongues' functions kerygmatically.
Snake-handling as protection-sign depends on the Mediterranean ecology in which venomous serpents were a real environmental threat.
The lethal-drink immunity sign reads against a background of persecution and poisoning-fears in the missionary situation.
Laying-on of hands as healing-gesture is a shared Second-Temple Jewish and Greco-Roman therapeutic convention.
Ascent-into-heaven presupposes the tiered-cosmos apocalyptic worldview where 'up' is where the divine throne is located.
'Sat at the right hand' draws on Near-Eastern royal-court honour-position imagery projected onto the divine throne.
The disciples' departure into wide-scale mission depends on Pax Romana road and sea networks that made such movement feasible.
'Preaching everywhere' rides on the pre-existing Jewish diaspora network as the initial venues of Christian proclamation.
'Confirmed by accompanying signs' defends the proclamation's authority against rival claimants in a competitive religious marketplace.
The formal closing formula reflects the manuscript-stratum's function of sealing the added ending as scripturally finished.

items.name: vindication-of-the-righteous-sufferer
items.evidence: 'Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised' — the announcement fuses the shameful execution and the divine reversal in a single breath, the classic Second-Temple pattern (cf. Wisdom 2–5, Daniel 12, the persecuted-then-exalted prophet) where God overturns the verdict of the powers on the innocent one.

items.name: royal-vindication-and-enthronement
items.evidence: ἠγέρθη (divine passive — God raises the condemned king); ἀνελήμφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐκάθισεν ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ (ascension + session at the divine right hand — Ps 110:1 enthronement script); τὸν ἐσταυρωμένον named as the subject of the announcement — the executed criminal is identified as the enthroned lord; τοῦ κυρίου συνεργοῦντος καὶ τὸν λόγον βεβαιοῦντος διὰ τῶν σημείων — the king ratifies his agents' word through signs, confirming ongoing sovereign authority
items.trans_sitz_note: The Longer Ending (⟦⟧) imports a Hellenistic wonder-worker (θεῖος ἀνήρ) paradigm that partially exceeds the text's indigenous Palestinian-Galilean repertoire. Exorcism and healing carry native Jewish warrant across multiple tradition-strata; but poison-immunity (θανάσιμόν τι πίωσιν οὐ μὴ βλάψῃ) and serpent-proof handling deployed as proofs of divine authorization belong more naturally to Greco-Roman aretalogical scripts in which bodily invulnerability demonstrates the holy man's ontological proximity to divinity (cf. Apollonius of Tyana traditions, Isis-Serapis miracle collections, Philostratean registers). The indigenous Jewish texts that approach this — Ps 91:13 ('you will tread on lion and cobra'), Elijah's invulnerability — frame divine protection differently: as narrative event within covenant history, not as a transferable credential-sign for commissioned agents. The Longer Ending's sign-list fuses the indigenous commission-paradigm with this Hellenistic authentication-script, slightly overcoding the native framework. Secondarily: individual resurrection before the general eschatological resurrection represents a minor but real trans_sitz innovation within Second Temple Jewish expectation — the text claims the general-resurrection script fires for one person ahead of schedule — but this strain is better described as internal theological extension than as importation from outside the tradition's own repertoire.

items.name: theophany-and-divine-commission

items.name: mourning-rite-and-lament-reversal
items.evidence: ἠγόρασαν ἀρώματα ἵνα ἐλθοῦσαι ἀλείψωσιν αὐτόν (women purchase spices for anointing — kinship-duty/purity body-preparation ritual); πενθοῦσι καὶ κλαίουσιν (mourning and weeping — full lament posture of the bereaved community); Τίς ἀποκυλίσει ἡμῖν τὸν λίθον ἐκ τῆς θύρας τοῦ μνημείου; (the nadir helplessness question — mourners blocked from completing the rite); stone already rolled away, body absent — the script's own telos (anointing the dead) is structurally impossible; the paradigm is invoked precisely to be broken open and redirect toward a different resolution entirely

tradition-register: angelic-figure in white garments (cf. Daniel 10:5–6; 2 Maccabees 3:26, 3:33; Genesis 18:2 LXX tradition)
tradition-register: angelophany 'fear not' commissioning formula (cf. Isaiah 41:10; 43:1; Daniel 10:12, 10:19; Judges 6:23; Tobit 12:17)
tradition-register: early kerygmatic belief-baptism-salvation formula (cf. Acts 2:38; Romans 10:9–10)
tradition-register: heavenly translation / bodily ascent of the righteous (cf. 2 Kings 2:11; Genesis 5:24 LXX; Sirach 48:9; 1 Maccabees 2:58)
tradition-register: prophetic indictment of hardness of heart / sklerokardia (cf. Ezekiel 3:7; Isaiah 6:9–10; Zechariah 7:11–12; Deuteronomy 10:16 LXX)
tradition-register: prophetic-mission closing affirmation / divine accompaniment of the sent (cf. Isaiah 55:11; Jeremiah 1:8, 1:19)
